chapter_title: Reading Analog Sensors with an ADC
chapter_summary:
The Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins are digital. They can only tell whether a signal is HIGH or LOW. Many sensors, however, produce analog signals that vary continuously. A potentiometer, a light-dependent resistor, and many temperature sensors all output analog voltages. To read these with a Raspberry Pi, you need an Analog-to-Digital Converter, or ADC.

An ADC measures an analog voltage and converts it into a digital number. A 10-bit ADC, such as the MCP3008, divides the input range into 1024 steps. If the reference voltage is 3.3V, a reading of 0 means 0V and a reading of 1023 means 3.3V.

The MCP3008 is a popular ADC for Raspberry Pi. It has eight input channels and communicates using the SPI protocol. SPI uses four wires: MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and CE0. On the Raspberry Pi, these are GPIO 10, GPIO 9, GPIO 11, and GPIO 8, respectively. You must enable SPI using `raspi-config` or the Raspberry Pi Configuration tool before using the MCP3008.

The wiring between an MCP3008 and a Raspberry Pi is as follows:

- MCP3008 VDD to 3.3V
- MCP3008 VREF to 3.3V
- MCP3008 AGND to GND
- MCP3008 CLK to GPIO 11 (SCLK)
- MCP3008 DOUT to GPIO 9 (MISO)
- MCP3008 DIN to GPIO 10 (MOSI)
- MCP3008 CS to GPIO 8 (CE0)
- MCP3008 DGND to GND

In Python, you can read the MCP3008 using the `gpiozero` `MCP3008` class:

```python
from gpiozero import MCP3008
from time import sleep

adc = MCP3008(channel=0)

while True:
    print(adc.value)
    sleep(0.5)
```

The `adc.value` property returns a number between 0 and 1. To convert it to a voltage, multiply by 3.3:

```python
voltage = adc.value * 3.3
print(f"Voltage: {voltage:.2f} V")
```

For a potentiometer connected across 3.3V and ground, the voltage at the wiper varies from 0V to 3.3V as you turn the knob. Reading this voltage lets you create a variable control for brightness, volume, or motor speed.

For a light-dependent resistor in a voltage divider with a fixed resistor, the voltage changes with light intensity. You can calibrate the sensor by recording the ADC value in bright light and in darkness, then map the range to a 0–100% scale.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn why the Raspberry Pi needs an ADC, and how the MCP3008 converts continuous voltages into digital numbers that the Pi can read. We start from the simple fact that the Pi's GPIO pins are digital — they only report high or low — and many sensors output a continuously varying voltage instead. That mismatch is solved by an Analog-to-Digital Converter. You will see the MCP3008, a widely used 10-bit ADC, wired to the Pi over the SPI protocol. We'll read values in Python using the gpiozero MCP3008 helper, convert those normalized readings into voltages, and use a potentiometer and an LED to demonstrate real control. Along the way I'll explain ADC resolution, reference voltage, and a simple calibration technique for a light sensor. By the end you'll understand the wiring, enabling SPI, the conversion math, and one practical project: a potentiometer controlling LED brightness. As you watch the terminal output and the wiring callouts, notice one common pitfall: mixing 5-volt sensors with a 3.3-volt reference. Keeping the reference and sensor supply consistent matters. Ready to explore how analog becomes digital and why that matters in your projects?

keyIdea.text: An ADC like the MCP3008 measures voltages in discrete steps so the Pi can read sensors that output continuous voltages.

screens.title: Why the Raspberry Pi Needs an ADC
screens.subtitle: Digital GPIO versus analog sensor outputs

narration.text: Start with the clear definition: the Raspberry Pi's GPIO pins are digital inputs and outputs. That means they tell you whether a signal is above or below a threshold — usually read as high or low — not the exact voltage level. Many sensors, like potentiometers, thermistors, and light-dependent resistors, produce a voltage that varies continuously with the measured quantity. An analog-to-digital converter, or ADC, measures that voltage and reports a discrete number the Pi can work with. A 10-bit ADC, such as the MCP3008, splits the input range into 1,024 steps. With a 3.3 volt reference, zero corresponds to zero volts and 1023 corresponds to 3.3 volts. A useful misconception to clear up is thinking you can read any analog pin directly: you cannot. The Pi needs an external ADC, or you must use sensors that provide digital outputs. A practical example: a potentiometer used as a volume knob will output a varying voltage on its wiper; the ADC reads this voltage and the Pi maps it to brightness or motor speed. Key takeaway: the ADC is the translator from continuous voltages into discrete numbers the Pi can understand. How would you test that translation on your bench right now?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: The ADC converts continuous voltages into discrete digital numbers so the Pi can measure analog sensors.

content.html:
Definition

Digital GPIO vs Analog Signals

Digital inputs report two states. Analog sensors output a voltage that varies with the measured quantity. An ADC bridges that gap.

Quick facts
  • 10-bit ADC → 1024 discrete steps.
  • Reference voltage sets full-scale mapping (commonly 3.3V).
  • Mixing 5V sensors with a 3.3V ADC risks damage.
Key Takeaway

An ADC is required to convert continuous voltages into numbers the Pi can process; resolution and reference determine precision.

Analogy

Analogy: measuring water level with steps

Imagine a tank with a continuous water level. An ADC is like a set of numbered steps; each step represents a small range of water heights. A 10-bit ADC gives you 1,024 steps to approximate the exact level.

Concrete example
Potentiometer wiper between 0 and 3.3V. ADC reading 512 corresponds to about 1.65 volts.
Common mistake
Expecting a Pi GPIO to return a voltage value. It returns high or low unless an ADC is used.
Check your understanding

If the reference is 3.3 volts and the ADC returns 1023, what is the input voltage? (Answer in the assessment later.)

screens.title: ADC Resolution and Reference Voltage
screens.subtitle: How bit depth and VREF determine measurement steps

narration.text: Let's unpack ADC resolution and reference voltage and why they matter in practice. Resolution refers to the number of distinct values an ADC can produce. A 10-bit ADC produces 1,024 steps because two to the power of ten is 1,024. If your reference voltage is three point three volts, then each step represents 3.3 divided by 1023, roughly three point two millivolts per step. That step size is the smallest voltage change the ADC can distinguish. The reference voltage defines what the maximum reading maps to; it must match the sensor supply or be a stable reference source. A common misconception is thinking that higher bit depth always fixes noisy measurements. Bit depth increases theoretical precision but does not reduce sensor noise or incorrect wiring. For a concrete example, a reading of 512 on a 10-bit ADC with a 3.3 volt reference corresponds to about one point six five volts. Practically, when choosing or interpreting ADC readings, consider both resolution and reference stability. Stable references and good grounding deliver dependable conversions. How will you check the step size on your board?

keyIdea.title: Resolution insight
keyIdea.text: Resolution and reference voltage together determine the ADC's step size and accuracy; compute volts = raw / 1023 * VREF.

content.html:
ADC Math

Resolution and VREF

Formula

Voltage = (raw_value / 1023) × VREF. For a 10-bit ADC, divide by 1023, not 1024, for correct full-scale mapping.

Step size

With VREF = 3.3V, step = 3.3 / 1023 ≈ 0.00322 V, or about 3.2 millivolts per step.

Worked example
If raw = 512, voltage ≈ 512 / 1023 × 3.3 ≈ 1.65 volts. This is the midpoint of the reference range and a useful sanity check when powering a potentiometer from 3.3V.
Why stability matters
A noisy or drifting VREF results in incorrect voltages even with high resolution.
Misconception
Higher bits don't fix a poor sensor or noisy wiring; they only increase numerical precision.
Check
Measure VREF with a multimeter before trusting conversions.
Visual
A vertical bar divided into 1024 steps labeled 0 and 1023 with VREF at top to visualize discrete steps across the voltage range.
Key Takeaway

Compute volts with the ADC formula and always verify your VREF and grounding for accurate readings.

screens.title: MCP3008 and SPI Overview
screens.subtitle: How the MCP3008 talks to the Raspberry Pi

narration.text: The MCP3008 is a practical choice for Raspberry Pi projects because it provides eight channels of 10‑bit ADC over SPI. SPI is a synchronous serial protocol using four signals: MOSI for data from the Pi to the device, MISO for data back to the Pi, SCLK for the clock, and CE or CS for chip select. On the Pi these are typically GPIO 10 (MOSI), GPIO 9 (MISO), GPIO 11 (SCLK), and GPIO 8 (CE0). The MCP3008 also needs power pins: VDD and VREF tied to 3.3 volts for proper scaling, plus AGND and DGND tied to ground. In operation, the Pi asserts chip select, toggles the clock, sends a command to choose a channel, and reads back the resulting 10-bit sample on MISO. A common misconception is confusing CE with power or assuming SPI is single-wire — it requires the four signals plus shared ground. A concrete example: to read channel zero the Pi initiates a transfer sequence that returns the 10-bit number for that channel. Understanding this handshake helps when debugging missing data or incorrect readings. MCP3008 and SPI Overview means mcp3008 provides 8 channels and uses spi's mosi, miso, sclk, and cs lines; vref sets the adc scale.. In practical terms, how the mcp3008 talks to the raspberry pi. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: MCP3008 architecture
keyIdea.text: MCP3008 provides 8 channels and uses SPI's MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and CS lines; VREF sets the ADC scale.

content.html:
Architecture

MCP3008 + SPI signals

The MCP3008 houses eight input channels and converts each selected channel to a 10-bit digital value sent over SPI. SPI is synchronous and requires explicit selection of the chip using CS.
SPI lines
  • MOSI — Pi to MCP3008
  • MISO — MCP3008 to Pi
  • SCLK — clock signal
  • CE/CS — chip select
Power pins
  • VDD → 3.3V
  • VREF → 3.3V
  • AGND, DGND → GND
Operational handshake

The Pi asserts CS, sends the channel selection sequence on MOSI while pulsing SCLK, then reads the 10-bit result on MISO. If CS is never asserted or wiring is wrong, reads fail or return noise.

Pin mapping (Pi → MCP3008)
GPIO 10 → DIN (MOSI), GPIO 9 → DOUT (MISO), GPIO 11 → CLK, GPIO 8 → CS (CE0). VDD and VREF to 3.3V, grounds tied together.
Key Takeaway

SPI is a four-wire synchronous link; correct wiring and stable VREF are essential for reliable ADC readings.

screens.title: Wiring the MCP3008 to the Raspberry Pi
screens.subtitle: Pin-to-pin connections and common wiring checks

narration.text: Wiring the MCP3008 correctly is a straightforward but critical step. Use the following mapping: MCP3008 VDD and VREF both to the Pi's 3.3 volt supply, AGND and DGND to ground, CLK to GPIO eleven, DOUT to GPIO nine, DIN to GPIO ten, and CS to GPIO eight. Always tie both analog and digital grounds to the Pi ground so the ADC has a common reference. After wiring, enable SPI in the Raspberry Pi OS by running the configuration utility and confirming SPI is active. A common mistake is connecting VREF to 5 volts when the Pi is 3.3 volts — this leads to damaging inputs or incorrect scaling. Another frequent issue is loose breadboard connections; press-fit wires can intermittently fail and show noisy values. A practical verification sequence is to first power the Pi and measure VREF with a multimeter to confirm 3.3 volts, then run a small read script to ensure you get stable values. If readings are noisy, recheck grounds, wiring, and ensure the sensor's supply matches VREF. How will you confirm your wiring before running code? Wiring the MCP3008 to the Raspberry Pi means vdd/vref→3.3v, agnd/dgnd→gnd, clk→gpio11, dout→gpio9, din→gpio10, cs→gpio8; verify 3.3v and common ground.. In practical terms, pin-to-pin connections and common wiring checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wiring checklist
keyIdea.text: VDD/VREF→3.3V, AGND/DGND→GND, CLK→GPIO11, DOUT→GPIO9, DIN→GPIO10, CS→GPIO8; verify 3.3V and common ground.

content.html:
Wiring

MCP3008 → Raspberry Pi mapping

  • MCP3008 VDD → Pi 3.3V
  • MCP3008 VREF → Pi 3.3V
  • MCP3008 AGND → Pi GND
  • MCP3008 DGND → Pi GND
  • MCP3008 CLK → Pi GPIO 11 (SCLK)
  • MCP3008 DOUT → Pi GPIO 9 (MISO)
  • MCP3008 DIN → Pi GPIO 10 (MOSI)
  • MCP3008 CS → Pi GPIO 8 (CE0)
After wiring, check VREF with a multimeter and ensure grounds are common. Tight breadboard connections and a stable power rail reduce noise and measurement errors.
Common mistakes
  • Using 5V for VREF while Pi runs at 3.3V.
  • Not tying analog and digital grounds together.
  • Loose breadboard or jumper wires causing intermittent reads.
Verification steps
  1. Power the Pi and measure the 3.3V rail at VREF.
  2. Confirm all grounds are common.
  3. Enable SPI in raspi-config and reboot.
  4. Run a quick read script and watch for stable values.
Key Takeaway

Correct wiring and verification eliminate the most common causes of bad ADC readings: incorrect VREF, missing grounds, and loose connections.

screens.title: Enable SPI on Raspberry Pi OS
screens.subtitle: Turn on the SPI interface and verify device availability

narration.text: Before the MCP3008 can communicate with the Pi, SPI must be enabled in the operating system. The standard way is to run the configuration utility and enable the SPI interface, then reboot. After reboot, use a quick system command to list SPI devices; you should see a device like spi0.0 when the driver is active. If the device is not present, revisit the configuration and confirm that the correct overlay is enabled and that your Pi model supports that SPI bus. A common misconception is thinking only code changes are needed; SPI must be enabled at the OS level so the kernel exposes the device node. As a quick verification, after wiring the MCP3008 and powering the Pi, run the listing command and then execute a short Python script that tries to open an MCP3008 object. If the object fails to open, check SPI enablement, wiring, and permissions. This step prevents hours of debugging when the physical wiring is correct but the OS is not configured to allow SPI access. Enable SPI on Raspberry Pi OS means enable spi in raspberry pi os and verify a spi device node exists before running adc code.. In practical terms, turn on the spi interface and verify device availability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SPI enablement
keyIdea.text: Enable SPI in Raspberry Pi OS and verify a spi device node exists before running ADC code.

content.html:
Enable SPI

OS-level enablement and verification

Use the Raspberry Pi configuration tool to enable SPI, reboot, then verify the kernel exposed an SPI device node such as spi0.0.
Verification steps
  1. Run the configuration tool and enable SPI.
  2. Reboot the Pi.
  3. List devices to confirm SPI appears (spi0.0).
  4. Run a short Python script to open the MCP3008 device and read a value.
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting to reboot after enabling SPI.
  • Not having the hardware header enabled on some Pi models.
  • Expecting code to work without kernel support for SPI.
Key Takeaway

Enabling SPI at the OS level is necessary for the MCP3008 to appear as a device the Python libraries can use.

screens.title: Reading the MCP3008 with gpiozero
screens.subtitle: A terminal-first Python example and voltage conversion

narration.text: We'll walk through a minimal Python pattern for reading an MCP3008 using the gpiozero package. The typical sequence is to import the MCP3008 class, instantiate it with a channel number, and then read the helper property that returns a normalized number between zero and one. Running a short loop that prints this value at half-second intervals gives you live feedback as you change the sensor. To derive a voltage, multiply that normalized value by the reference voltage, usually three point three volts. A useful concrete example: set up the MCP3008 on channel zero, run the loop, and watch the printed output move between near zero and near one as you turn a potentiometer. One common confusion is the difference between 'raw' ADC counts and the normalized value returned by the helper class; the gpiozero class abstracts the raw integer into a floating point between zero and one. If you need the raw counts, the library offers lower-level access or you can scale the normalized value by 1023 to recover a typical 10-bit reading. To solidify understanding, try printing both the normalized value and the calculated voltage and check that the midpoint corresponds to roughly one point six five volts.

keyIdea.title: Reading pattern
keyIdea.text: Use gpiozero's MCP3008 to get a normalized value, then multiply by VREF to obtain voltage; inspect both normalized and raw scales for clarity.

content.html:
Code Example

Python terminal demo

from gpiozero import MCP3008
from time import sleep

adc = MCP3008(channel=0)

while True:
    value = adc.value  # normalized 0.0 - 1.0
    voltage = value * 3.3
    print(f"raw: {value:.3f}  voltage: {voltage:.2f} V")
    sleep(0.5)
The example prints a normalized value and a calculated voltage. If you need raw counts on a 10-bit ADC, multiply the normalized value by 1023 and round to an integer.
Concrete check
If the printed voltage reads about 1.65 V at midpoint, the conversion and wiring are likely correct.
Misconception
Do not assume adc.value is a raw integer; it is normalized. Convert if you require the actual 10-bit count.
Terminal demo
Run the example in a terminal to observe live readings as you change sensor inputs. This instant feedback is the fastest way to verify wiring and conversion math.
Key Takeaway

Use the helper to get normalized values, convert to volts by multiplying by VREF, and confirm midpoint values for sanity checking.

screens.title: Potentiometer to PWM LED Project
screens.subtitle: Read the wiper, convert to voltage, and control LED brightness

narration.text: This hands-on activity turns theory into action: wire a potentiometer across 3.3 volts and ground, connect the wiper to channel zero of the MCP3008, and read the value in Python. Use the reading to drive a PWM output that controls an LED's brightness. The flow is: read adc. value, scale or map the normalized value to a PWM duty cycle, and write it to a PWM-capable GPIO pin. A concrete mapping is simple: duty_percent = adc. value × 100. One practical detail is that the PWM frequency and LED current-limiting resistor determine the perceived smoothness and safety of the LED. A common mistake is driving a high-power LED directly from a GPIO without a transistor or driver — always use appropriate current control. Another pitfall is mixing sensor supply rails; ensure the potentiometer, MCP3008 VREF, and Pi GPIO all share the same 3.3-volt reference. After you run the program, rotating the potentiometer should smoothly change LED brightness. If brightness jumps or the terminal reads noisy values, check wiring, grounding, and VREF stability. Try logging both normalized value and duty cycle to verify your mapping.

keyIdea.title: Project pattern
keyIdea.text: Read ADC value, map to PWM duty, and use safe driving hardware for LEDs; keep supplies and reference consistent.

content.html:
Project

Potentiometer → ADC → PWM LED

Wire the potentiometer between 3.3V and ground, with the wiper to MCP3008 channel 0. Read adc.value and map it to PWM duty cycle to control LED brightness safely.
Simple mapping example
value = adc.value  # 0.0 - 1.0
duty_percent = value * 100  # 0 - 100%
# write duty_percent to a PWM output pin via a safe driver
Safety tip
Use a transistor or LED driver and a current-limiting resistor to avoid damaging the Pi GPIO.
Debug tip
If brightness is erratic, check VREF and ground connections for noise or floating pins.
Concrete scenario
Connect LED to a transistor, control transistor base with a PWM GPIO, and read ADC to vary duty cycle in real time.
Key Takeaway

Mapping ADC readings to PWM controls a physical output; always use proper drivers and confirm reference consistency.

screens.title: LDR and Voltage Divider Calibration
screens.subtitle: Mapping light sensor readings to a 0–100% scale

narration.text: A light-dependent resistor changes resistance with light, so we typically use it in a voltage divider with a fixed resistor to create a measurable voltage. To calibrate the sensor, record ADC readings in known conditions: bright light and dark. These two recordings give you the min and max raw values. Use linear mapping to convert any intermediate raw reading into a percentage: percent = (reading - min) / (max - min) × 100, clamped to zero and one hundred percent. A concrete calibration routine is: place the sensor in bright daylight and note the ADC value, then block the sensor and note the darkness value. Save these values in your program and use them to display a percent reading. A common mistake is trusting default resistor choices for your light range; the fixed resistor should be chosen so the divider output moves substantially across the ADC range for expected lighting conditions. If the sensor saturates at one extreme, pick a different fixed resistor or change placement. Calibration converts raw numbers into meaningful units for display or decision-making. LDR and Voltage Divider Calibration means record min and max adc readings in known conditions and map intermediate readings to 0–100% for meaningful results.. In practical terms, mapping light sensor readings to a 0–100% scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Calibration method
keyIdea.text: Record min and max ADC readings in known conditions and map intermediate readings to 0–100% for meaningful results.

content.html:
Calibration

LDR in a voltage divider

Choose a fixed resistor so the divider voltage spans a useful portion of the ADC range in your lighting conditions. Then record extremes and map the readings to percent.

Calibration example
bright_value = read_adc(); dark_value = read_adc() in darkness; percent = (value - dark_value) / (bright_value - dark_value) * 100
Concrete step
Record and save calibration values rather than hard-coding them every run to improve accuracy.
Adjustment tip
If readings saturate, change the fixed resistor value so the divider output shifts within the ADC range.
Real-world use
Calibrated light percentages are useful for UI elements, thresholds, or logging environmental data consistently across devices.
Key Takeaway

Calibration turns raw ADC counts into meaningful percentages by recording extremes and mapping intermediate values linearly.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Measurement Accuracy
screens.subtitle: Grounding, reference, wiring, and interpreting noisy readings

narration.text: When ADC readings are incorrect or noisy, several common causes account for most problems. First, missing or floating ground connections produce unpredictable values; always tie AGND and DGND to the Pi ground. Second, mismatched reference voltages — for example powering a sensor at five volts while VREF is three point three volts — yields out-of-range or damaging conditions. Third, loose breadboard connections or long unshielded wires introduce noise. Fourth, assuming high bit depth solves noise: it does not; you must address noise sources with proper wiring, decoupling capacitors on the power rails, and stable references. Compare two scenarios: a well-wired system with common ground, short wires, and stable VREF will show smooth ADC transitions as a potentiometer is turned. A poorly wired system shows sporadic jumps and inconsistent midpoints. To test accuracy, measure VREF with a multimeter, read a fixed known voltage and confirm the expected ADC raw or normalized value, and log readings over time to check for drift. A small oscilloscope or logic analyzer helps diagnose timing and noise issues but is optional for basic troubleshooting. What step will you take first to improve a noisy reading?

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting summary
keyIdea.text: Check grounds, VREF consistency, wiring security, and address noise sources; measure known voltages to validate conversions.

content.html:
Comparison

Healthy vs Problematic ADC reads

Healthy setup
Common ground, VREF tied to 3.3V, short wiring, stable readings, smooth potentiometer response.
Problematic setup
Floating ground, VREF mismatch, long wires, unstable readings, and noisy or jumping values.
Practical checks
  • Measure VREF with a multimeter and confirm 3.3V.
  • Read a known voltage and compare expected ADC value.
  • Inspect and shorten wiring; add decoupling if needed.
Key Takeaway

Most ADC problems are wiring and reference issues. Verify those first, then examine noise and timing if needed.

Second, ADC resolution and reference voltage together determine measurement step size and scale; compute volts by dividing the raw count by the full scale and multiplying by the reference. Third, the MCP3008 uses SPI and requires correct VDD, VREF, ground, and the four SPI lines to operate. Each concept is a practical checkpoint: ensure you have the right interface, compute conversions properly, and wire the chip correctly before running code. Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts — Part 1

Analog vs Digital

Analog sensors output continuous voltages; the Pi needs an ADC to read those values numerically.

ADC Resolution & VREF

Resolution sets steps, VREF sets scale; volts = raw / 1023 × VREF for a 10-bit ADC.

MCP3008 + SPI

MCP3008 has eight channels and communicates via MOSI, MISO, SCLK, and CS; tie VREF to 3.3V when using a Pi.

Takeaway

Keep these three concepts in mind as you wire, code, and calibrate to prevent common errors and ensure accurate readings.

narration.text: A final set of three practical reminders will help your lab work. First, always verify the Pi's three point three volt rail and common ground before trusting ADC conversions. Second, use gpiozero's MCP3008 helper for normalized readings but understand how to recover raw counts if needed; multiply by 1023 to see 10-bit integers. Third, calibrate sensors such as potentiometers and LDRs by recording extremes and mapping intermediate values into percentages. These checks prevent common errors: incorrect scale, mistaken counts, and uncalibrated sensor outputs. Practically, before running any code: check VREF, confirm SPI is enabled, and run a short terminal loop to watch live readings as you move the sensor. That quick routine saves time and keeps your hardware safe. Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Practical Reminders

Key Concepts — Part 2

Verify power & ground

Confirm 3.3V at VREF and tied grounds to ensure meaningful ADC conversions.

Use gpiozero

The MCP3008 class returns normalized values; multiply by 3.3 to get volts or by 1023 to get raw counts.

Calibrate sensors

Record min and max ADC readings under known conditions and map values to a percentage scale.

Final tip

Before running projects, do a three-point check: power rails, SPI enablement, and a terminal demo that shows live ADC values while moving the sensor.
